title: HTML5 Foundations
description: Learn the semantic building blocks of the web. Move beyond basic tags and understand how to structure accessible, SEO-friendly documents.

lessons.title: The HTML Boilerplate
lessons.explanationHtml:
Every HTML document starts with a standard boilerplate. This includes the <!DOCTYPE html> declaration which tells the browser to use HTML5 standards, the <html> root element, the <head> for metadata, and the <body> for visible content.

Understanding this structure is critical because placing scripts or styles in the wrong section can severely impact page load performance.

Recommended Resource

HTML Tutorial for Beginners - Programming with Mosh

lessons.title: Semantic HTML vs Divs
lessons.explanationHtml:
A common beginner mistake is using a <div> for everything. Semantic HTML means using tags that convey meaning to the browser and to screen readers.

Using tags like <header>, <main>, <article>, and <footer> instantly improves your website's accessibility and Search Engine Optimization (SEO).

Recommended Resource

Semantic HTML - Kevin Powell

lessons.title: Forms & User Input
lessons.explanationHtml:
Forms are how users interact with your backend. HTML5 introduced powerful new input types like email, date, and number that come with built-in browser validation.

Always wrap your inputs in a <form> tag and use <label> tags linked via the for attribute. This makes the inputs clickable via the label text, which is vital for mobile users and accessibility.
lessons.codeExample:
<form action="/api/submit" method="POST">
  <label for="email">Email Address:</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
  
  <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>

lessons.title: Images & Accessibility
lessons.explanationHtml:
The <img> tag embeds images into your page. However, an image without an alt attribute is a massive accessibility failure.

The alt text is read by screen readers for visually impaired users, and it is displayed if the image fails to load. If the image is purely decorative, you should still include an empty alt attribute: alt="".

lessons.title: Hyperlinks & Navigation
lessons.explanationHtml:
The anchor tag <a> is what makes the web a "web". It links pages together.

Use the href attribute to specify the destination. If you want the link to open in a new tab, use target="_blank", but always pair it with rel="noopener noreferrer" to prevent security vulnerabilities.

lessons.title: Organizing Data with Lists
lessons.explanationHtml:
When presenting sequential data or a group of related items, use lists instead of consecutive paragraph tags.

HTML provides <ul> for unordered (bulleted) lists, <ol> for ordered (numbered) lists, and <dl> for description lists. Navigation menus are almost always built using an unordered list!

lessons.title: Building Accessible Tables
lessons.explanationHtml:
In the 1990s, tables were used for page layout. Today, they should ONLY be used for tabular data.

A correct table uses <thead> for the headers, <tbody> for the data rows, and <th> tags for column headers. This structure allows screen readers to announce the column name as the user navigates through cells.

lessons.title: Meta Tags for SEO
lessons.explanationHtml:
What happens when someone shares your link on Twitter or iMessage? The preview card is generated by <meta> tags in your <head>.

You must include a description meta tag, and ideally Open Graph (og:) tags. This drastically improves click-through rates and SEO rankings.
lessons.codeExample:
<head>
  <meta name="description" content="Learn HTML5 with this comprehensive guide.">
  <meta property="og:title" content="HTML5 Foundations">
  <meta property="og:image" content="/assets/html5-banner.png">
</head>

title: Modern CSS & Layouts
description: Stop struggling with centering divs. Master Flexbox, CSS Grid, variables, and responsive design to build layouts that look incredible on any device.

lessons.title: The Box Model
lessons.explanationHtml:
Every element in CSS is a rectangular box. The Box Model consists of four layers: the actual content, padding (space inside the border), the border itself, and margin (space outside the border).

A critical best practice is applying box-sizing: border-box; to all elements. This ensures that adding padding doesn't accidentally increase the total width of your element, preventing horizontal scrolling bugs.

Recommended Resource

CSS Box Model - Web Dev Simplified

lessons.title: Flexbox Fundamentals
lessons.explanationHtml:
Flexbox was designed for one-dimensional layouts (either a row or a column). It solves the historical nightmare of vertical alignment.

By setting display: flex; on a container, you unlock powerful alignment properties like justify-content (main axis) and align-items (cross axis).

Recommended Resource

Flexbox Crash Course - Traversy Media

lessons.title: Mastering CSS Grid
lessons.explanationHtml:
While Flexbox is one-dimensional, CSS Grid is designed for two-dimensional layouts (rows AND columns simultaneously).

Grid is perfect for page layouts, dashboard shells, and complex photo galleries. The fr (fraction) unit is your best friend here, allowing columns to proportionally share available space.

lessons.title: CSS Custom Properties (Variables)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Stop hardcoding colors! CSS Variables (Custom Properties) allow you to define a value once and reuse it everywhere. If the client wants to change the brand color from blue to purple, you only have to change one line of code.

Variables are defined with a double hyphen -- and are typically placed in the :root pseudo-class so they are globally accessible.

lessons.title: Responsive Design & Media Queries
lessons.explanationHtml:
Your website will be viewed on devices ranging from 320px wide to 4K monitors. Media queries allow you to apply CSS only when the screen matches certain conditions.

Best Practice: Use a "mobile-first" approach. Write your default CSS for mobile phones, and use min-width media queries to add complexity for larger screens.

lessons.title: Pseudo-classes (:hover, :focus)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Pseudo-classes describe the special state of an element. The most common is :hover, which triggers when the user's mouse is over the element.

Equally important is :focus-visible, which highlights an element when a user tabs to it using a keyboard. Never remove focus outlines without providing a custom alternative, as it destroys keyboard accessibility.

lessons.title: Transitions & Animations
lessons.explanationHtml:
Motion gives your interface a premium feel. Use the transition property for simple state changes (like hovering a button).

For complex, looping, or multi-step animations, use @keyframes. Always stick to animating transform and opacity whenever possible, as animating properties like width or margin forces the browser to expensively recalculate the layout (reflow).

lessons.title: Z-Index & Stacking Contexts
lessons.explanationHtml:
Ever set a z-index to 99999 and the element STILL sits behind something else? That's because of Stacking Contexts.

Z-index only works on positioned elements (relative, absolute, fixed, sticky) or flex/grid children. Furthermore, z-index values are trapped within their parent's stacking context. If a parent has a low z-index, no child can break out to be above elements outside that parent.

title: JavaScript Core
description: Learn the programming language of the web. Move past basic syntax to truly understand closures, async programming, and DOM manipulation.

lessons.title: Variables: let, const, and var
lessons.explanationHtml:
In modern JavaScript (ES6+), you should almost never use var. It is function-scoped and leads to unpredictable bug due to 'hoisting'.

Always default to const. Only use let if you know the variable's value needs to be reassigned later (like in a for-loop or an accumulator). This forces you to write more predictable code.

Recommended Resource

Let vs Const vs Var - Web Dev Simplified

lessons.title: Arrow Functions & 'this'
lessons.explanationHtml:
Arrow functions () => {} provide a shorter syntax, but their most important feature is how they handle the this keyword.

Traditional functions create their own this context, which often causes bugs when passed as callbacks. Arrow functions implicitly inherit this from the surrounding scope (lexical scoping).

lessons.title: Higher-Order Array Methods
lessons.explanationHtml:
Stop using for loops to transform data. Array methods like .map(), .filter(), and .reduce() are declarative—they describe WHAT you want to do, not HOW to loop.

Mastering these three methods is an absolute prerequisite before moving into frontend frameworks like React.

lessons.title: Destructuring & Spread Operator
lessons.explanationHtml:
Destructuring allows you to unpack values from arrays or properties from objects directly into distinct variables. It makes your code significantly cleaner.

The spread operator ... expands an iterable (like an array or object) into its individual elements. It is heavily used for cloning objects and merging arrays.

lessons.title: Promises & Async/Await
lessons.explanationHtml:
JavaScript runs on a single thread. If you make a network request and wait for it synchronously, the entire website freezes. To solve this, JS uses asynchronous code.

A Promise represents the eventual completion (or failure) of an asynchronous operation. async/await is syntactical sugar that makes reading Promise-based code look identical to synchronous code.

Recommended Resource

Async/Await - Fireship

lessons.title: DOM Manipulation
lessons.explanationHtml:
The Document Object Model (DOM) is a tree representation of your HTML that JavaScript can interact with.

Using document.querySelector(), you can select any element using CSS selectors, and then manipulate its text, classes, or styles. This is the foundation of making web pages interactive.

lessons.title: Understanding Closures
lessons.explanationHtml:
A closure happens when a function "remembers" the variables in its lexical scope, even after the outer function has finished executing.

Closures are frequently used to emulate private methods, create factory functions, and manage state in React Hooks.

lessons.title: Event Bubbling & Delegation
lessons.explanationHtml:
When you click an element, that click event "bubbles" up the DOM tree, triggering click listeners on all its parent elements.

Instead of attaching 100 event listeners to 100 list items, you can attach ONE event listener to the parent <ul> and use event.target to figure out which child was actually clicked. This is called Event Delegation.
